SURGO × UNIVERSITY OF MANITOBA · SENEGAL

Demand, services and modern contraceptive use

Women’s own reported concerns are examined alongside the recorded service environment where they live. Looking at both can identify places where social support, service improvements or integrated responses warrant attention.

Initial evidence: personal concern profiles, especially opposition and anticipated stigma, are associated with lower modern use after adjustment. The selected supply score’s independent association remains uncertain. Geographic profiles identify relative concerns and service weaknesses; they do not establish causal binding constraints.

Women and facilities overlap in 33 departments

The individual-level join retains all 7,169 original women. Manitoba contains 2,043 facility records across 46 departments: 33 also have SURGO respondents, and 13 have facilities only. The map shows source coverage before restricting the analytical population.

Residence-classification limitation and decision. Facility Rural/Urban labels come from a health-district lookup, not a directly verified settlement classification for each facility. In Mbacke, all 64 facility records are Urban-labelled, while SURGO contains 529 Urban and 253 Rural women. Urban women receive the Urban-labelled facility profile; Rural women receive a flagged department-wide fallback. Among women with FPN2 = 1, this is 136 Urban women and 56 Rural women. The department-wide and Urban-labelled profiles are numerically identical here. This does not prove that rural services are absent or that Rural women attended Urban facilities.

This rule applies to 1,815 source women across 16 departments, including 522 women in need. The remaining 1,383 women in need have exact department–residence profiles. No unmatched measure is coded zero. Existing profiles with an unanswered component would retain that missing component; the fallback rule is triggered by an absent geographic profile.

02 · USE, INTENTION AND METHOD CHOICE

Among women SURGO classifies as in need of family planning

Population used from this section onward: original SURGO FPN2 = 1, exactly as recorded in the source survey. This gives 1,905 women. No older script’s need_n recoding or sterilization/hysterectomy additions are applied. Eleven nonconsenting records are outside estimation and have FPN2 = 95.

Every bar and sub-bar has the same denominator: all 1,905 women with FPN2 = 1. Percentages use WEIGHT; n is an unweighted respondent count. Capped whiskers are 95% logit intervals using the available RB0H census-district design, constructed before domain selection. Original sampling strata and finite-population corrections are unavailable. Subsets overlap: modern users are included in current users, so these bars do not sum to 100%. 4 users have unresolved modern/traditional classification; 98 have another or unresolved initiation-preference response. *Preference concerns the method wanted at initiation; the type of alternative wanted is not established. Future intention concerns any method, without a specified 12-month initiation window.

Initial pattern. Weighted current use is 50.4%, including 45.9% modern use. Another 17.1% are nonusers with intention and 32.3% nonusers without stated intention. These groups help distinguish existing use from stated future interest without treating this cross-sectional survey as a transition study.

How each comparison method works
ApproachScore constructionFlagging threshold
Rank averageRank departments separately for each component, using average ranks for ties; average six ranks on each side.Demand above its final-score median; favorable supply below its median.
Mean percentagesAverage the six original percentages separately on each side.Same strict final-score median rule.
Median/IQRFor each component, subtract its department median and divide by its IQR; average six transformed values.Same strict final-score median rule.
Median countCount components above the demand component medians, or below the favorable supply component medians.Flag at least four of six unfavorable comparisons.
Z-score average · primaryFor each component, subtract its department mean and divide by its sample SD; average six component z-scores.Same strict final-score median rule.

These are relative planning classifications, not validated service-adequacy thresholds. Every component receives equal weight. Exact median ties are unflagged. Rankings order the final scores; the map uses the continuous z-score averages and their score medians, not an additional ranking cutoff.

Five-method comparison ↓Exact thresholds ↓Component values and transformations ↓

Department planning profiles · z-score average

How the scores and map thresholds are constructed
  1. Summarize each department. Demand inputs are six WEIGHT-weighted concern percentages among valid FPN2 = 1 women. Supply inputs are six unweighted facility summaries using all facilities within each department.
  2. Standardize each component across the 33 linked departments. Calculate (department value − department mean) ÷ sample SD. Each department contributes equally to this reference. Higher demand values mean more concern; higher raw supply values mean stronger provision.
  3. Average six standardized components on each side. This gives department demand and favorable supply-readiness scores. These contextual demand scores are used for the map; the models instead use each woman’s own responses.
  4. Apply separate final-score medians. Flag demand strictly above 0.058673. Flag supply readiness strictly below 0.018123, equivalent to supply risk above -0.018123. Exact ties are not flagged.

Both flags → Both; one flag → Demand only or Supply only; no flags → Neither flagged. The 13 facility-only departments are outside the demand/supply comparison. “Neither flagged” does not establish adequate services or no barriers. Small samples do not change these relative scores or thresholds.

Both: 8Demand only: 8Supply only: 8Neither flagged: 9Facility data only: 13

Planning signal. Among the 33 linked departments, 8 have both sides flagged, 8 demand only, 8 supply only, and 9 neither. Use the component priorities below to identify what should be investigated in each place; a category alone is insufficient to choose an intervention.

04 · ADJUSTED ASSOCIATIONS

Modern use in relation to personal concerns and local services

All models: 1,445 women with original SURGO FPN2 = 1, including 737 modern users across 33 departments. Outcome: current modern use = 1; confirmed traditional-only use or nonuse = 0. Adjust for age + age², Senegal-specific education, partnership, fertility goal and Rural/Urban residence. Use WEIGHT, department-clustered CR2/Satterthwaite intervals, and no random effects or interactions.

Score assigned to each womanConstructionObserved model variation
Demand risk scoreStandardize her own six demand responses using weighted item means and population SDs among valid FPN2 = 1 women; average all six. Her department or residence does not determine this score.61 distinct values across 1,445 women.
Supply risk scoreStandardize her assigned six residence-specific or flagged department-fallback measures against the fixed 33-department planning means/SDs. Average and reverse the sign: higher = weaker provision.39 distinct numeric scores across 49 department–residence contexts; 402 modeled women receive fallbacks.
ModelPredictors alongside the same covariates
1 · Demand scorePersonal demand score
2 · Supply scoreAssigned supply risk score
3 · Both scoresPersonal demand score + assigned supply risk score
4 · Six demand indicatorsEach woman’s six demand indicators separately
5 · Six indicators + supplySix personal demand indicators + assigned supply risk score

Key finding. In Model 3, the demand odds ratio is 0.27 (0.20–0.35) and the supply risk odds ratio 0.75 (0.43–1.31) per one original average-z index point. The demand association remains after accounting for recorded supply and covariates. The supply interval includes 1, so its independent association remains uncertain. These do not allocate a percentage of nonuse to either side.

Planning interpretation. The curves show how predicted modern use varies with each score for the same women, holding other predictors at their observed values. Their levels and uncertainty are easier to interpret than odds ratios. They are adjusted cross-sectional comparisons, not expected gains from removing barriers. An uncertain supply slope does not establish adequate services.

Which reported concerns accompany lower use?

Models 4 and 5 retain personal responses separately. Model 5 also includes the same contextual supply score. The supply-only model is Model 2, shown again for reference.

Key finding. In Model 5, opposition to family planning has OR 0.11 (0.06–0.22); anticipated stigma has OR 0.56 (0.38–0.80). The six demand coefficients are jointly associated with use (Holm p <0.001). Use the heatmap to locate these concerns alongside service weaknesses; these associations do not establish which intervention would be most effective.

What this means for planning. The adjusted present-versus-absent difference is -41.3 percentage points for opposition and -11.6 points for anticipated stigma. The model predicts the same women under each response setting, retains their supply and other characteristics, and averages using WEIGHT. These gaps identify patterns to investigate; they are not intervention-effect estimates.

DEFINITIONS AND VERIFICATION

How to interpret the measures and their limits

Demand variables and missing-response rules
IndicatorSource and interpretation
Healthcare permission barriersHS7C: 1 = permission to seek a doctor is a challenge; 2 = no. General healthcare permission, not FP-specific partner approval.
Anticipated social stigmaPB7B/C: 1/2 on either item, concerning being seen by someone known or what people would say. Zero requires both valid negatives (3/4); unresolved responses remain missing unless the other item establishes concern.
Health / side-effect beliefsPB2A–C: 1/2 on any item about health problems, reduced sexual desire or malformed babies; zero requires all valid 3/4 responses. Bleeding is excluded. These are perceived beliefs, not clinically verified effects.
Future-fertility concernsAny MP4_a–f selected for later childbearing concerns about reversible methods. Require coherent MP4_a–i 0/1 responses, at least one selection or explicit none, no none-plus-method contradiction, and MP4_99 = 0. Sterilization items MP4_g/h do not create a fertility concern; unknown responses are not zero.
Low method knowledge · retained labelMC5A/B: 3/4 on either item, measuring low confidence choosing a suitable method or handling side effects/switching. This is self-efficacy/confidence, not an objective knowledge test. Zero requires both valid 1/2 answers.
Opposes family planningFP1: 3/4 = against versus 1/2 = in favor. Unfamiliarity, no opinion and other special codes remain unresolved.

These modules have responses among current users and nonusers and are not restricted to married women. Special codes are excluded from valid item denominators. A known positive can establish an any-concern flag; zero requires valid negatives on every included item. Do not interpret unresolved responses as absence of concern.

FP1’s unclassifiable responses comprise unfamiliarity (5) and no opinion (99), rather than only “don’t know”. MP4 is one multiple-response question; its “don’t know” option governs interpretation of the method selections.

Health and fertility account for most unresolved domains. PB2B (reduced sexual desire) has 403 “don’t know” answers; PB2C (malformed babies) has 385; PB2A (health problems) has 113. A known concern on another item can still establish a positive health flag, leaving 264 health domains unresolved overall. MP4_99 is explicitly “don’t know which methods could affect later fertility”: 244 women select it, including two who also select a method. Confidence has 34 unresolved domains. FP1 has 17 unfamiliarity and 9 no-opinion responses, which cannot be classified as either opposition or support.

These are largely substantive uncertainty responses, not necessarily data errors. The binary concern scores do not assign uncertainty a risk value. Coding unknowns as no concern is unsupported; excluding them may select a more informed subset. Department percentages use valid domain responses, while the primary models require a complete personal profile. Counts overlap across domains; the percentages above use WEIGHT.

Supply variables and denominators
IndicatorCalculation and interpretation
Short + long-acting offeringAverage one_larc_3_sa_offer, joined as share_offer_larc_and_3_sa. Share meeting the original ≥1 long-acting plus ≥3 short-acting product/category rule. Higher = stronger recorded provision.
Free-product provisionAverage valid facility p_free_prod proportions, joined as mean_p_free_prod. A value of 60% means the average reporting facility provides 60% of its recorded products free; it is not the percentage of facilities offering any free method.
Trained-provider shareAverage valid facility p_train proportions, joined as mean_p_train. Describes the average reporting facility’s trained-personnel proportion under the original UoM eligibility; not the share of facilities with at least one trained provider.
FP counselor availabilitySenegal item s7_2: Yes/(Yes+No), joined as share_fp_counselor. Codes 1 = Yes; 0/2 = No; unknown responses excluded. Availability is not counseling receipt or quality. Reporting coverage is sparse.
At least one LARC in stockAverage one_larc_stockin, joined as share_stocked_1plus_larc. Share meeting the original at-least-one-long-acting-product stock rule. The three-LARC measure is constant FALSE and cannot be standardized.
Most-popular product in stockn_mp_in_stock_true/(true+false). Percentage among facilities with known status, each facility referring to its own most-popular product. This does not measure each woman’s preferred method.

No facility sampling weights are constructed. Valid-response aggregation follows the existing UoM facility definitions. A missing answer is not automatically evidence of no provision. The same definitions are applied within departments and within department–residence cells, before assigning profiles to women.

Original SURGO need classification and analytical population

Sections 2 onward use original FPN2 = 1, with original WEIGHT and consent. The source records 1,905 women as in need, 5,253 as not in need and 11 nonconsenting records with code 95. Among the 7,158 consenting positive-weight respondents, the weighted in-need share is 27.2%. This report does not reconstruct that flag, use an older researcher’s need_n, add permanent-protection cases, or apply DHS unmet-need coding. All original survey fields, including FPN2, are independently verified as unchanged.

Survey design, adjustment and common model sample

Use WEIGHT from the Senegal source. The available survey design uses RB0H, explicitly labelled census district, with 118 recorded clusters among consenting respondents; cluster nesting in departments and residence is verified. Construct the full consenting positive-weight design before selecting FPN2 = 1. Original sampling strata and FPC are not documented in the supplied materials, so complete reconstruction of the original complex design cannot be claimed.

Models retain these weights and use department-clustered CR2 covariance with coefficient-specific Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Sampling-census-district survey-GLM intervals are exported as an inference sensitivity; weighted point estimates agree. The models adjust for age + age², education (primary or less; middle/secondary; tertiary/professional), partnership, fertility goal (five categories including after marriage and uncertain), and FV_MILIEU Rural/Urban. There are no random effects or interactions.

There are 39 distinct numeric supply scores across 49 woman-occupied department–residence contexts, and 33 departments for clustered inference. Fallbacks can equal an Urban-labelled profile numerically; this does not create new independent supply information. The joint z-score supply coefficient has 9.0 effective degrees of freedom. Diagnostics and VIF checks are not a formal power guarantee. Cross-sectional associations do not identify causal mechanisms, and current experience can influence reported beliefs. Confidence intervals condition on the estimated scores.

APPENDIX · PCA SENSITIVITY

Alternative scores using the same individual and contextual inputs

Separate weighted correlation PCAs summarize the same six personal demand indicators and six assigned supply measures. Both are restricted to original FPN2 = 1 women. Demand PCA uses 1,451 complete women; supply PCA uses 1,905 women across 49 residence/fallback source profiles, weighted by their represented women’s summed WEIGHT. These are not facility weights.

What PCA captures. Demand PC1 retains 24.8% of demand variation; supply PC1 retains 34.7%. In this Senegal fit, all PC1 coefficients are positive after orientation. Demand PC1 emphasizes opposition, low confidence and stigma; supply PC1 emphasizes offering and LARC stock. The model negates favorable supply PC1 to obtain supply risk. These coefficients describe variation in inputs, not their effects on modern use.

Use final-weighted input means/population SDs, eigendecompose the standardized correlation matrix, and project each woman’s own demand responses or assigned supply inputs onto PC1. PC1 is prespecified as a sensitivity; no outcome-informed coefficients or PCA geographic categories are constructed. Demand PC2 also retains variation, so PC1 is not a complete summary of every domain.

Exploratory 2,000-permutation and leave-one-department-out construction checks are available. Repeated fallback/Urban-equivalent profiles do not provide independent new areas; permutation references are construction diagnostics, not survey-design tests. Model intervals condition on the estimated scores. PCA units differ from average-z units, so odds-ratio magnitudes across methods cannot establish which fit is stronger.

The same five modern-use models using PCA scores

All models: 1,445 women with original SURGO FPN2 = 1, including 737 modern users across 33 departments. Outcome: current modern use = 1; confirmed traditional-only use or nonuse = 0. Adjust for age + age², Senegal-specific education, partnership, fertility goal and Rural/Urban residence. Use WEIGHT, department-clustered CR2/Satterthwaite intervals, and no random effects or interactions.

ModelPredictors alongside the same covariates
1 · Demand scorePersonal demand score
2 · Supply scoreAssigned supply risk score
3 · Both scoresPersonal demand score + assigned supply risk score
4 · Six demand indicatorsEach woman’s six demand indicators separately
5 · Six indicators + supplySix personal demand indicators + assigned supply risk score

Key finding. In Model 3, the demand odds ratio is 0.50 (0.43–0.59) and the supply risk odds ratio 0.89 (0.74–1.06) per one oriented PC1 unit. The demand association remains after accounting for recorded supply and covariates. The supply interval includes 1, so its independent association remains uncertain. These do not allocate a percentage of nonuse to either side.

Planning interpretation. The curves show how predicted modern use varies with each score for the same women, holding other predictors at their observed values. Their levels and uncertainty are easier to interpret than odds ratios. They are adjusted cross-sectional comparisons, not expected gains from removing barriers. An uncertain supply slope does not establish adequate services.

Which reported concerns accompany lower use?

Models 4 and 5 retain personal responses separately. Model 5 also includes the same contextual supply score. The supply-only model is Model 2, shown again for reference.

Key finding. In Model 5, opposition to family planning has OR 0.11 (0.06–0.22); anticipated stigma has OR 0.56 (0.39–0.81). The six demand coefficients are jointly associated with use (Holm p <0.001). Use the heatmap to locate these concerns alongside service weaknesses; these associations do not establish which intervention would be most effective.

What this means for planning. The adjusted present-versus-absent difference is -41.2 percentage points for opposition and -11.4 points for anticipated stigma. The model predicts the same women under each response setting, retains their supply and other characteristics, and averages using WEIGHT. These gaps identify patterns to investigate; they are not intervention-effect estimates.
